title: How migrating European robins sense Earth's magnetic field (cryptochrome; Oldenburg electromagnetic noise study)

sources.title: Man-Made Electromagnetic Noise Disrupts a Bird's Compass (2014)
Everyday electronics may upset birds' compass (2014-05-08)
A proposed 'quantum compass' for songbirds just got more plausible (2021-06-28)

facts.text: European robins are migrating songbirds that travel at night.
European robins have a built-in compass that detects Earth's magnetic field, which helps them keep their direction even when they cannot see the sun, moon, stars or landmarks.
During the migration season, caged migratory birds tend to hop and face in the direction they would fly.
In a classic test, a bird is put in a funnel-shaped cage lined with paper that keeps the marks of its feet, showing which direction it tries to go.
A leading idea is that a protein called cryptochrome in birds' eyes works as the magnetic sensor; the idea was proposed in 2000 and is still debated.
When light hits cryptochrome, an electron moves within the protein, leaving two unpaired electrons.
Earth's weak magnetic field can affect how this electron pair behaves and so change the outcome of the protein's chemical reactions.
In a 2021 laboratory study, cryptochrome 4 from European robins responded to magnetic fields, while the same protein from chickens and pigeons, which do not migrate, showed little effect.
Scientists still do not know how the bird perceives the signal from the protein.
Starting in 2004, robin experiments at the University of Oldenburg in Germany stopped working: the birds could not orient, and for about three years the team could not find out why.
In 2006 the team put a grounded aluminum screen around the birds' hut to block electromagnetic noise, and the robins' compass started working again right away.
The disturbing noise came from electronic equipment in use on campus and was 100 to 1,000 times weaker than the human exposure limits recommended by the World Health Organization.

Researchers said that such weak fields should not affect living tissue, so the result supports the idea that the bird compass relies on a very sensitive quantum process such as the cryptochrome mechanism.
When the huts were moved to a rural spot about 1 kilometer outside the city, the robins oriented normally without the screen.
It is not clear whether wild birds are affected; a bird with a disturbed compass can still use the sun and stars, but under cloudy skies a faulty compass might matter more.
The Oldenburg results were published in the journal Nature in 2014 after seven years of repeated, double-blind tests.
